newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu goes on offensive against PLO.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu goes on offensive against PLO.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday defended the start of work on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem and went on the offensive against the PLO, accusing it of backing "terrorism".

Asked at a news conference if the construction would end the peace process, Netanyahu said: "Absolutely not. And I recommend to all parties concerned to stop this hyperbole...I'm sure the peace process will continue."

But he warned the PLO that a resumption of suicide bombings in Israel by Moslem militants could kill peace efforts already strained by Israel's plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews at Jabal Abu Ghneim, or Har Homa in Hebrew.
Netanyahu said the Palestinian Authority had recently released jailed members of Hamas, the militant Islamic group responsible for suicide bombings that killed 59 people in Israel last year.

"I am saying that our intelligence shows very clearly, unmistakably, that the Palestininan leadership has given the green light to the worst terrorist organisations in the world to go ahead with the kind of bus bombings and suicide attacks -- the kind of mass killings that brought a halt to the peace process," he said.

Hours earlier, Netanyahu told reporters during a tour of the southern Israeli town of Dimona: "We will be unable to continue the peace process if we are threatened with terror attack or made to absorb terror attacks."
At the news conference in Jerusalem, the right-wing leader said Israel has "a right to build in Jerusalem...we are going to do it."
"If we are willing to surrender on the issue of Jerusalem, we will surrender everything," Netanyahu said.

Israel regards all of the city, including the eastern sector captured in the 1967 Middle East war, as its "eternal and indivisible capital". The PLO wants East Jerusalem to be the capital of a Palestinian state.
Netanyahu urged the Palestinian Authority, in charge of parts of the West Bank and Gaza, not to encourage violence in protest at the settlement project.
"I've urged restraint to our security forces," he said.
Other Israeli officials, however, said the army would respond forcefully to any Palestinian violence.
Last September 61 Arabs and 15 Israelis were killed in clashes that erupted after Netanyahu opened another entrance to an archaeological tunnel near Moslem holy sites in East Jerusalem.
"What I seek...indeed is a dialogue both with Chairman (Yasser) Arafat and with the Palestinian Authority at every level," Netanyahu said. "Unfortunately the door was shut."
"He has basically refused any contact," Netanyahu said.

Aides to the Palestinian president said a summit would be conditioned on an Israeli pledge to freeze construction of the settlement, another link in a chain of Israeli apartment blocks nearly encircling East Jerusalem.
